summary:
Nepal criminalises no conduct on the basis of gender identity or gender expression. Same-sex acts have been legal since the Supreme Court's December 2007 judgment in Sunil Babu Pant v. Nepal Government, which held that homosexuality is not 'unnatural'. The Criminal Codes Act 2017, which replaced the 1963 Muluki Ain, still lists 'unnatural sex' on its face and must be read in light of that ruling; the former Muluki Ain criminalised 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to one year's imprisonment, and LGBTQI+ Nepalis were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition rests on the 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognising the right to self-determined name and gender markers, and a third-gender category has been available on official documents by self-declaration. In August 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed more than 50 lawsuits from 2021 onward. Before that ruling, changing a marker to female or male had usually required surgery performed outside the country followed by in-country medical evaluations, including intrusive post-operative genital examinations.

The documentary pathway remained unclear at the level of ordinary administration. In February 2024 Human Rights Watch called on the government to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure for transgender and third-gender people to obtain official documents, indicating that no straightforward document-change process existed at that date. Reporting in February 2024 separately documented that officials limited marker changes to people identifying as 'third gender', while changes to male and female markers lagged behind the country's progressive reputation.

Visibly trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are frequently subjected to physical and sexual harassment, including in provincial cities such as Janakpur, according to reporting from November 2024. LGBT children encounter discrimination at school and leave education because of threats, bullying and neglect by fellow students and teachers, and trans Nepalis face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, particularly in rural areas.

Partner recognition is partial and contested. On 28 June 2023 Justice Til Prasad Shrestha issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities, and the full bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024 the National ID and Civil Registration Department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register. Temporary registration confers no equal rights: same-sex couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions or adopt children, and certificates label them 'groom and bride'. The first marriage of a trans woman and a cisgender man took place in November 2023, and as of June 2025 the Blue Diamond Society counted at least 17 documented queer marriages. Implementation is inconsistent: the Kathmandu District Court rejected a registration in July 2023, and compliance by local governments is unknown. Suman Pant's Supreme Court case set a precedent for same-sex spousal visas.

Gender-affirming care is newly established and thin. The first gender-affirming surgery in Nepal was performed in June 2025 at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, which has since established a Gender Affirming Clinic. Hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery remain hard to reach: a six-month hormone supply costs 4,500 rupees, providers are few, and many trans Nepalis take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma; some travel to India and Thailand for surgery. Conversion therapy is practised, including treatment in rehabilitation centres and traditional exorcism by family members, and lesbian couples are denied IVF.

Official hostility has surfaced alongside the protective rulings. On 30 October 2024 the Aamul Paribartan Nagarik Party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, and Mitini Nepal's executive director stated that anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in Nepal and South Asia. In April 2026 newly elected Prime Minister Balen Shah faced LGBTQ community criticism over a YouTube rap video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; after demands for an apology, his supporters markedly increased derogatory comments, hate speech and death threats against the community. The Communist Party of Nepal-Maoist made homophobic statements during the Civil War, describing homosexuality as 'a production of capitalism' and LGBT people as 'social pollutants'.

Two protective measures are on record but not verified as implemented: UNDP has recommended that transgender and intersex students be given access to safe toilets and bathroom facilities, and the Education Board has implemented information about sexual and gender diversity in the curriculum for grades 7–9 (ages 13–15), making Nepal the second Asian country after Mongolia to do so, with universities offering courses on LGBT issues.
tangentialFactors:
Nepal's international standing as a progressive jurisdiction on sexual orientation and gender identity has repeatedly been described as running ahead of policy on the ground, with observers noting that the country's reputation needs to be matched with real policy and that an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans community.

Social conditions have been documented as resistant to the legal framework across time: a 2015 study found that sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation, and a 2020 assessment by local queer organisations reached a comparable conclusion about the distance between constitutional right and statute.

Community organisations provide the main service infrastructure. The Blue Diamond Society operates a drop-in centre with free HIV testing in Kathmandu and has more than 50 branches, while Mitini Nepal, Parichaya Samaj and Sahaayam Nepal also provide resources. Queer Youth Group has filed writ petitions at the Supreme Court demanding legal recognition of gender identity and has advocated for the citizenship bill.

Public visibility is established but contested. Pride events held annually include the Nepal Pride Parade (since 2019), Queer Womxn Pride and the Trans Pride Parade (since 2020). Media representation of LGBT people has historically been negative or comic relief, with caricatures of transgender people, gay people and lesbians, though positive depictions include Highway (2012) and Soongava (2012); Nepali media has also been criticised for forcefully using 'third gender' to describe trans men and trans women, and some observers have accused media and activists of pinkwashing and spreading disinformation about same-sex marriage and LGBT rights.
localsOnly:
Citizenship documentation has been a sustained focus of local advocacy: Queer Youth Group has advocated for the citizenship bill alongside its Supreme Court writs, and civil society produced a Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078 in October 2021 through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship, authored by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi.

During the 2011 census some enumerators demanded that a child be stripped when parents listed them as 'third gender', an episode that bears on how third-gender markers are handled in official enumeration.

Healthcare and support services available to residents include the drop-in centre with free HIV testing run by the Blue Diamond Society in Kathmandu, its network of more than 50 branches, and the resources of Mitini Nepal, Parichaya Samaj and Sahaayam Nepal. Research and healthcare addressing LGBT Nepalis' needs are described as severely lacking, and many trans Nepalis take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma.

Education content on sexual and gender diversity is in the curriculum for grades 7–9 (ages 13–15), and universities offer courses on LGBT issues, though LGBT children still leave school because of threats, bullying and neglect by fellow students and teachers.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening rules for trans travellers, including whether passport or citizenship markers are checked on arrival. That layer is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved rather than as absent.

Whether the August 2024 Supreme Court ruling in Rukshana Kapali's favour has been generalised into a standing administrative procedure for other applicants is not established by these sources; the February 2024 Human Rights Watch statement describes the position before that ruling, and no post-ruling assessment of routine practice is available.

The final verdict of the full bench on same-sex marriage registration remains pending, and compliance by local governments with the April 2024 instruction to maintain a separate register is unknown. Whether the temporary registration framework recognises marriages involving a trans spouse on the same terms as other couples is not sourced.

No source addresses hate-crime legislation covering gender identity or expression, the legality of conversion therapy, conditions of detention for trans people, or access to identification documents for non-citizens. These are unresolved, not confirmed absent.

The April 2026 account of Prime Minister Balen Shah's video and the subsequent online abuse rests on community criticism and reporting of that criticism; no official response or investigation is documented in this inventory.
